extracted.intended_audience: nonprofit organizations, grant writers, and fundraisers seeking grant funding
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for nonprofit organizations and grant writers on common reasons grant proposals fail and how to improve proposals to increase chances of funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: You didn't follow the guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders expect you to be scrupulous in adhering to their guidelines. They expect you to meet all eligibility requirements. They expect you to have adequate support personnel to operationalize the plans as set forth in your proposal. Most important, before they even open a proposal, they expect it to be submitted on time!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully review the “eligibility” section of all requests for proposals (RFPs). Don’t waste time pursuing grants you’re not eligible for; if you don’t meet all requirements, consider partnering with another organization that better fits the criteria. Follow solicitations meticulously; read your final proposal several times and present ideas clearly, concisely, and logically. If you don’t get the grant, ask the funder why — their feedback can be invaluable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your proposal is too vague
rubrics_metrics.description: Your proposal may not clearly outline the specifics that the funder is looking for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sure to specify your target population; details of the activities that will take place; and exactly how and where service recipients will be served. Read the proposal as if hearing the ideas for the first time to ensure clarity about mutual expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The focus of the proposal may be too narrow
rubrics_metrics.description: The population you’re targeting may not be large enough. The grantor may feel the services you’re proposing aren’t widespread enough to make a significant, measurable impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design projects so they will demonstrate measurable impact across a sufficiently large or appropriate population; if the scope is too limited, funders may conclude it won’t meaningfully address the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: The proposal may be too broad
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals such as eliminating societal ills like hunger and poverty are too unrealistic to be practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed goals must be achievable, reachable, doable, and measurable. Avoid overly ambitious, vague world-changing claims; instead set realistic, specific objectives with measurable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your organization doesn’t have a significant enough track record to be considered credible
rubrics_metrics.description: If your organization isn’t well known or lacks a strong track record, funders may doubt your credibility and ability to manage funds and achieve goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even new organizations should establish credibility—partner with established, reputable organizations if needed. Demonstrate fiduciary responsibility, relevant knowledge, skills, and experience so funders feel confident they will get what they pay for.

rubrics_metrics.name: You haven't presented a clear evaluation plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Grantors want accountability: they need to know how you will show whether you accomplished the goals stated in your proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify how you will measure success, what kinds of measures you will use, and whether measures will be generated and presented by an internal or external evaluator. Describe systems and processes in place to accurately measure and report accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances beyond your control may prevent funding
rubrics_metrics.description: External factors can block funding even for excellent proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include budget cuts that cause funders to withdraw or scale back grants, or a funder changing its focus or priorities. Recognize that even the best proposal can be declined for reasons unrelated to proposal quality; persist and continue refining and resubmitting.
